clears: Somebody handling them: “No wall was lifted, stacked or knocked by anybody.”
d.note: The same two walls are the thin ones, the cold ones and the ones on stone, so every difference lands on the same pair. That is the hardest shape a case can take and it is worth naming. The sentence about uneven cooling is the rule in the story, and the stone answer is the only one that uses it directly.

title: The Case of the Half-Dark String
story: Half the hallway light string went dark and the other half stayed lit. The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth. Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn. When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out. The lit half is wired as its own separate line. Mr. Cole tested the outlet and it carried full power. He checked the plug and the cord and found no break or fray. The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken. Every other bulb in the dark half tested fine in a working socket.
q: Why did half the string go dark?

sus.why: when one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line goes out
he tested the outlet and it carried full power
he found no break or fray
every other bulb in the dark half tested fine

ans: One broken bulb opened the line that half the string runs on.
proof: “When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out.”
“The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”
clears: The outlet: “Mr. Cole tested the outlet and it carried full power.”
A break in the cord: “He checked the plug and the cord and found no break or fray.”
All the bulbs: “Every other bulb in the dark half tested fine in a working socket.”
explain: Twenty-five bulbs went out and twenty-four of them still work. Because that half is one line with the current running through every bulb in turn, the single broken filament at number twenty-six is enough to darken all of them.

d.story: Half the hallway light string went dark and the other half stayed lit. The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth. Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn. When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out. The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken. The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it. A bulb that is not seated breaks the line as surely as a broken filament does. Water from a leaking window ran down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty. The outlet reads full power on the tester and runs the lit half fine.
d.q: Why did half the string go dark? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a twenty-sixth bulb that rattles, with a broken filament
an outlet that tested at full power
a cracked socket where the bulb sits loose
water running down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty

evidence: “The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”
“When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out.”
args.against: “The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it.”

evidence: “The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it.”
“A bulb that is not seated breaks the line as surely as a broken filament does.”
args.against: “The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”

evidence: “Water from a leaking window ran down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty.”
“The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth.”
args.against: “Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn.”

clears: The outlet: “The outlet reads full power on the tester and runs the lit half fine.”
d.note: Everything in this case points at bulb twenty-six and the class should say so before arguing. The question underneath is what caused what: a cracked socket lets a bulb rattle, rattling breaks a filament, and water gets into a cracked socket. Ordering those three is the real work, and the story deliberately leaves the order out.

title: The Case of the Clock That Lost Four Minutes
story: The hallway clock lost about four minutes a day all through January. It had kept time to the second for the six years before that. The battery tested at full voltage and the hands moved freely. Nothing was rubbing the hands and the glass had not been struck. This clock keeps time with a thin metal wheel that turns at a fixed rate. Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly. The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December. A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January. The identical clock at the far end of the hall kept perfect time.
q: Why was the clock losing time?

sus.why: metal expands when it warms and turns more slowly
the battery tested at full voltage
nothing was rubbing the hands
it had kept time to the second for six years

ans: Heat from the radiator expanded the wheel and slowed the clock.
proof: “Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly.”
“A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January.”
clears: A weak battery: “The battery tested at full voltage and the hands moved freely.”
Something rubbing: “Nothing was rubbing the hands and the glass had not been struck.”
A faulty clock: “It had kept time to the second for the six years before that.”
explain: Six perfect years, then four minutes a day the month a radiator went in underneath it. Because the wheel that sets the rate runs slower as it warms, ninety-four degrees is enough to cost four minutes every day.

d.story: The hallway clock lost about four minutes a day all through January. For six years before that it had not drifted by a second. This clock keeps time with a thin metal wheel that turns at a fixed rate. Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly. The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December. A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January. The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares. A battery that reads full voltage can still fail under load. The identical clock at the far end of the hall was also rehung in December. That one hangs over the stairwell, where the air is cold and still. The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.
d.q: Why did the clock lose four minutes a day? Make the case for one cause.

sus.why: a new radiator below it, and ninety-four degrees beside it
a December battery from the drawer of mixed spares
nothing rubbing the hands and no struck glass
rehung in December, over a radiator rather than a cold stairwell

evidence: “The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December.”
“A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January.”
args.against: “The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares.”

evidence: “The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares.”
“A battery that reads full voltage can still fail under load.”
args.against: “Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly.”

evidence: “The identical clock at the far end of the hall was also rehung in December.”
“That one hangs over the stairwell, where the air is cold and still. The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.”
args.against: “For six years before that it had not drifted by a second.”

clears: Something rubbing the hands: “The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.”
d.note: The second clock used to be a clean control and it has stopped being one, because it was also rehung in December and it is also somewhere with a temperature. It is still useful, just not as proof. Three things changed in December and only one of them is measured, which is why the thermometer reading carries the most weight.

title: The Case of the Snow That Melted in Stripes
story: Snow on the playground melted in stripes and left white bands between them. The bare stripes sit directly over the black rubber safety mat. The white bands sit over the light grey concrete beside it. Air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground. Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth. Light surfaces throw much of the same sunlight away again. A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete. The snow fell evenly, and a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn. No salt, sand or shovel had been anywhere near the playground all winter.
q: Why did the snow melt in stripes?

sus.who: ⬛ The dark rubber mat taking in sunlight
sus.why: the rubber read fifty-one and the concrete thirty-six
no salt, sand or shovel had been near the playground
a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn
air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground

ans: The dark rubber mat took in sunlight and melted the snow above it.
proof: “Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth.”
“A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete.”
clears: Salt: “No salt, sand or shovel had been anywhere near the playground all winter.”
Uneven snowfall: “The snow fell evenly, and a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn.”
Warmer air: “Air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground.”
explain: The air was the same everywhere and the ground was not. Because the black mat sat at fifty-one degrees while the concrete sat at thirty-six, the snow melted exactly where the dark surface was and nowhere else.

d.story: Snow on the playground melted in stripes and left white bands between them. The bare stripes sit directly over the black rubber safety mat. The white bands sit over the light grey concrete beside it. Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth. Light surfaces throw much of the same sunlight away again. A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete. The heating pipe to the gym runs under the rubber strip and not under the concrete. A buried pipe warms the ground above it whatever the sun is doing. The rubber strip is a hand's width lower than the concrete and water collects along it. A ruler at dawn showed the same depth of snow everywhere on the playground.
d.q: Why did the snow melt in stripes? Choose one cause and quote the story.

sus.who: ⬛ The dark rubber mat taking in sunlight
sus.why: fifty-one degrees on the dark rubber against thirty-six on the concrete
no salt, sand or shovel near the playground all winter
a gym heating pipe running under the rubber and not the concrete

sus.who: 💧 A lower strip that collects water
sus.why: a strip a hand's width lower, where water collects

evidence: “Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth.”
“A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete.”
args.against: “The heating pipe to the gym runs under the rubber strip and not under the concrete.”

evidence: “The heating pipe to the gym runs under the rubber strip and not under the concrete.”
“A buried pipe warms the ground above it whatever the sun is doing.”
args.against: “Light surfaces throw much of the same sunlight away again.”

evidence: “The rubber strip is a hand's width lower than the concrete and water collects along it.”
“Snow on the playground melted in stripes and left white bands between them.”
args.against: “A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete.”

clears: Uneven snowfall: “A ruler at dawn showed the same depth of snow everywhere on the playground.”
d.note: The thermometer reading is real and it does not say why the rubber is warm. Sun and a buried pipe both produce exactly that reading, which is the trap. Ask what would separate them, and the class should arrive at reading the same two surfaces at night, when the sun is not a candidate at all.

title: The Case of the Feeder Nobody Visited
story: The window feeder emptied in two days all autumn and sat full for a week in November. The seed was the same mix from the same sack. The feeder hung in the same spot at the same height. No seed was spoiled and the ports were clear of ice. Small birds will leave a feeder that has no cover within a short flight. They need somewhere to dart to when a hawk passes overhead. The lilac hedge eight feet from the feeder was cut back hard on the first of November. The nearest cover now stands forty feet away across open lawn. Birds were still seen in the yard all week.
q: Why did the birds stop using the feeder?

sus.why: small birds leave a feeder with no cover within a short flight
no seed was spoiled and the ports were clear of ice
the seed was the same mix from the same sack
birds were still seen in the yard all week

ans: Cutting the lilac hedge left the feeder with no cover nearby.
proof: “They need somewhere to dart to when a hawk passes overhead.”
“The lilac hedge eight feet from the feeder was cut back hard on the first of November.”
clears: Spoiled seed: “No seed was spoiled and the ports were clear of ice.”
A different mix: “The seed was the same mix from the same sack.”
The birds leaving: “Birds were still seen in the yard all week.”
explain: Same seed, same feeder, same birds in the yard. Because safe cover went from eight feet to forty on the first of November, the feeder became a place small birds will not risk sitting at.

d.story: The window feeder emptied in two days all autumn and sat full for a week in November. Small birds will leave a feeder that has no cover within a short flight. They need somewhere to dart to when a hawk passes overhead. The lilac hedge eight feet from the feeder was cut back hard on the first of November. The nearest cover now stands forty feet away across open lawn. A sparrowhawk has been seen on the fence three mornings running since the hedge came down. The window behind the feeder was fitted with reflective film on the second of November. Birds avoid a feeder they cannot see a clear escape from. Birds were about the yard all week, on the fence and on the grass. A fresh sack was opened on the first and the ports are clear of ice.
d.q: Why did the birds stop using the feeder? Pick one cause and prove it.

sus.why: a hedge cut back hard, leaving cover forty feet away
seed unspoiled and ports clear of ice
a sparrowhawk on the fence three mornings running
reflective film fitted to the window behind it

evidence: “The lilac hedge eight feet from the feeder was cut back hard on the first of November.”
“The nearest cover now stands forty feet away across open lawn.”
args.against: “The window behind the feeder was fitted with reflective film on the second of November.”

evidence: “A sparrowhawk has been seen on the fence three mornings running since the hedge came down.”
“They need somewhere to dart to when a hawk passes overhead.”
args.against: “Birds were about the yard all week, on the fence and on the grass.”

evidence: “The window behind the feeder was fitted with reflective film on the second of November.”
“Birds avoid a feeder they cannot see a clear escape from.”
args.against: “The lilac hedge eight feet from the feeder was cut back hard on the first of November.”

clears: Spoiled or blocked seed: “A fresh sack was opened on the first and the ports are clear of ice.”
d.note: The hedge came down on the first and the film went up on the second, which is as close as two causes can get without being the same day. The hawk is downstream of the hedge, and a good answer says so rather than treating it as a third option. Birds still in the yard is the fact that keeps all three alive.

title: The Case of the Lumpy Cocoa
story: Two pitchers of cocoa were mixed side by side and one came out full of lumps. Both used four scoops of the same powder and the same milk. Both were stirred for the same ninety seconds with the same whisk. Dry powder clumps when a lot of liquid hits it all at once, because the outside of each clump turns to paste and seals the dry middle in. Adding a little liquid first makes a smooth paste that then thins out safely. Ms. Baptiste poured half a cup into the first pitcher and stirred before adding the rest. The whole quart went into the second pitcher at once. Neither pitcher was heated and neither sat before serving.
q: Why was one pitcher lumpy?

sus.who: 🫗 Pouring the whole quart in at once
sus.why: the outside of each clump turns to paste and seals the dry middle in
both were stirred the same ninety seconds
both used four scoops of the same powder
neither pitcher was heated

ans: The whole quart hit the dry powder at once and sealed the lumps in.
proof: “Adding a little liquid first makes a smooth paste that then thins out safely.”
“The whole quart went into the second pitcher at once.”
clears: Not enough stirring: “Both were stirred for the same ninety seconds with the same whisk.”
Old powder: “Both used four scoops of the same powder and the same milk.”
Heating it: “Neither pitcher was heated and neither sat before serving.”
explain: Same powder, same milk, same ninety seconds of whisking. Because the first pitcher got a little liquid and a stir before the rest, its powder never had the chance to seal itself into lumps the way the second one's did.

d.story: Two pitchers of cocoa were mixed side by side and one came out full of lumps. Dry powder clumps when a lot of liquid hits it all at once, because the outside of each clump turns to paste and seals the dry middle in. Adding a little liquid first makes a smooth paste that then thins out safely. Ms. Baptiste poured half a cup into the first pitcher and stirred before adding the rest. The whole quart went into the second pitcher at once. The second pitcher's powder came from the bottom of the tin, which had set hard in places. The second whisk has three bent wires and does not reach the pitcher's corners. Both were stirred for the same ninety seconds.
d.q: Why was one pitcher lumpy? Argue for one cause.

sus.who: 🫗 Pouring the whole quart in at once
sus.why: a whole quart poured in at once, sealing the dry middles in
ninety seconds of stirring in both pitchers
powder from the bottom of the tin, set hard in places
a whisk with three bent wires that misses the corners

evidence: “The whole quart went into the second pitcher at once.”
“Adding a little liquid first makes a smooth paste that then thins out safely.”
args.against: “The second pitcher's powder came from the bottom of the tin, which had set hard in places.”

evidence: “The second pitcher's powder came from the bottom of the tin, which had set hard in places.”
“Two pitchers of cocoa were mixed side by side and one came out full of lumps.”
args.against: “The whole quart went into the second pitcher at once.”

evidence: “The second whisk has three bent wires and does not reach the pitcher's corners.”
“Dry powder clumps when a lot of liquid hits it all at once, because the outside of each clump turns to paste and seals the dry middle in.”
args.against: “Both were stirred for the same ninety seconds.”

clears: Not enough stirring: “Both were stirred for the same ninety seconds.”
d.note: Ninety seconds each clears the stirring time and does not clear the whisk, which is a distinction worth drawing out: the same time with a worse tool is not the same stirring. Powder set hard in a tin already contains lumps before any liquid arrives, and a student who spots that has found the one answer that does not need the pouring at all.

title: The Case of the Valentines in the Wrong Bags
story: Every valentine in Room 7 landed in the wrong bag on Friday afternoon. Each one was off by exactly the same distance down the row. Nobody opened a card and nothing was missing or torn. The bags hang in a fixed order along the back wall. That order is alphabetical by last name and has not changed all year. The class list taped to the table is alphabetical by first name instead. The helper worked straight down the printed list and straight along the wall. The two orders put a different child in the same position almost everywhere. The helper had never delivered the valentines before that day.
q: Why did every card land in the wrong bag?

sus.why: the wall is by last name and the list is by first name
nobody opened a card
that order has not changed all year
nothing was missing or torn

ans: The helper matched a first-name list against last-name bags.
proof: “That order is alphabetical by last name and has not changed all year.”
“The class list taped to the table is alphabetical by first name instead.”
clears: Somebody opening them: “Nobody opened a card and nothing was missing or torn.”
The bags being moved: “The bags hang in a fixed order along the back wall.”
Missing cards: “nothing was missing or torn.”
explain: Nothing was lost and nothing was opened, and every card is off by the same amount. Because the list and the wall are sorted two different ways, working carefully down both at once puts every single card in somebody else's bag.

d.story: Every valentine in Room 7 landed in the wrong bag on Friday afternoon. The bags hang along the back wall in an order set in September. That order is alphabetical by last name and has not changed all year. The class list taped to the table is alphabetical by first name instead. The helper worked straight down the printed list and straight along the wall. The two orders put a different child in the same position almost everywhere. Two bags fell off their hooks on Thursday and were rehung by whoever found them. Four children have the same first initial and their bags carry no photograph. Not one card was opened, and none went missing or came back torn.
d.q: Why did every valentine land in the wrong bag? Make the case for one cause.

sus.why: a wall by last name and a list by first name, worked straight down
nobody opening a card, and nothing missing or torn
two bags that fell on Thursday and were rehung by whoever found them
four children sharing an initial, with no photograph on a bag

evidence: “That order is alphabetical by last name and has not changed all year.”
“The class list taped to the table is alphabetical by first name instead.”
args.against: “Two bags fell off their hooks on Thursday and were rehung by whoever found them.”

evidence: “Two bags fell off their hooks on Thursday and were rehung by whoever found them.”
“The bags hang along the back wall in an order set in September.”
args.against: “Every valentine in Room 7 landed in the wrong bag on Friday afternoon.”

evidence: “Four children have the same first initial and their bags carry no photograph.”
“The helper worked straight down the printed list and straight along the wall.”
args.against: “The two orders put a different child in the same position almost everywhere.”

clears: Somebody opening the cards: “Not one card was opened, and none went missing or came back torn.”
d.note: Every card went wrong, and the word every is the whole argument. Two rehung bags move two cards. Four shared initials confuse four. Only two lists in different orders can put the entire class out at once, and a student who reasons from how many each cause would spoil has found the method this case is really teaching.

title: The Case of the Volcano That Would Not Erupt
story: Four model volcanoes erupted at the fair and the fifth only fizzed. All five used two spoons of baking soda and half a cup of vinegar. The soda and the vinegar came from the same two containers. Baking soda and vinegar make gas, and the gas is what pushes the foam up. Baking soda left open to damp air slowly reacts and loses its power. The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September. Its surface was crusted and clumped rather than loose and powdery. The fifth cone was built to the same height and the same opening. The vinegar in the fifth cup still smelled as sharp as the rest.
q: Why did the fifth volcano only fizz?

sus.who: 🥄 Baking soda spoiled by damp air
sus.why: its surface was crusted and clumped
the vinegar still smelled as sharp as the rest
built to the same height and the same opening
all five used two spoons and half a cup

ans: The fifth team's baking soda had already reacted in damp air.
proof: “Baking soda left open to damp air slowly reacts and loses its power.”
“The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September.”
clears: Weak vinegar: “The vinegar in the fifth cup still smelled as sharp as the rest.”
A badly built cone: “The fifth cone was built to the same height and the same opening.”
Wrong amounts: “All five used two spoons of baking soda and half a cup of vinegar.”
explain: Same recipe, same cone, same vinegar. Because soda left open in damp air spends its power before it ever reaches the cup, two spoons of crusted soda cannot make the gas that four spoons of fresh soda made.

d.story: Four model volcanoes erupted at the fair and the fifth only fizzed. Baking soda and vinegar make gas, and the gas is what pushes the foam up. Baking soda left open to damp air slowly reacts and loses its power. The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September. Its surface was crusted and clumped rather than loose and powdery. The fifth team used a tall narrow cone with an opening the width of a thumb. A narrow opening slows foam down however much gas is made. The fifth cup of vinegar was poured at eight in the morning and used at two. Vinegar left standing in an open cup loses sharpness through the day. Each of the five measured two spoons of soda and half a cup of vinegar.
d.q: Why did the fifth volcano only fizz? Pick one cause and prove it.

sus.who: 🥄 Baking soda spoiled by damp air
sus.why: soda open on a humid porch since September, crusted and clumped
vinegar poured at eight and used at two, standing open
a tall narrow cone with an opening the width of a thumb
two spoons and half a cup, the same as the other four

evidence: “The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September.”
“Its surface was crusted and clumped rather than loose and powdery.”
args.against: “The fifth cup of vinegar was poured at eight in the morning and used at two.”

evidence: “The fifth cup of vinegar was poured at eight in the morning and used at two.”
“Vinegar left standing in an open cup loses sharpness through the day.”
args.against: “Its surface was crusted and clumped rather than loose and powdery.”

evidence: “The fifth team used a tall narrow cone with an opening the width of a thumb.”
“A narrow opening slows foam down however much gas is made.”
args.against: “Baking soda and vinegar make gas, and the gas is what pushes the foam up.”

clears: Wrong amounts: “Each of the five measured two spoons of soda and half a cup of vinegar.”
d.note: Two of these say less gas was made and one says the gas could not get out, which is a real difference worth naming. A narrow cone would still fill and hiss; weak ingredients would not. Ask what the fizz actually looked like, and notice that the case never says, which is a fair complaint to make about the evidence.

title: The Case of the Crown That Would Not Close
story: Twenty paper crowns were cut to one pattern and six would not close. The six that failed were all cut by the same two students. Every crown came off the same roll of card at the same width. Nobody trimmed, tore or re-cut any crown after it was measured. A head is measured around, and that measurement is the length the strip must reach. The pattern sheet lists the head width across instead of the distance around. A circle's distance around is a little more than three times its width. The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need. The other fourteen students measured around with a tape as instructed.
q: Why would six crowns not close?

sus.why: the distance around is a little more than three times the width
nobody trimmed, tore or re-cut any crown
every crown came off the same roll at the same width
twenty crowns were cut to one pattern

ans: Six students measured the head across rather than around.
proof: “The pattern sheet lists the head width across instead of the distance around.”
“The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need.”
clears: Trimming them short: “Nobody trimmed, tore or re-cut any crown after it was measured.”
A narrower roll: “Every crown came off the same roll of card at the same width.”
A different pattern: “Twenty paper crowns were cut to one pattern and six would not close.”
explain: A third is the number that gives it away. Because the distance around a circle is a bit over three times the distance across, a crown measured across comes out at almost exactly a third of the length it needed.

d.story: Twenty paper crowns were made from one pattern and six will not close. The six that failed were all cut by the same two students. A head is measured around, and that measurement is the length the strip must reach. The pattern sheet lists the head width across instead of the distance around. A circle's distance around is a little more than three times its width. The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need. The card ran out and the last roll is two inches narrower than the first. Two pattern sheets sit in the folder and the older one is for a smaller size. The six failed crowns were cut on the afternoon the second sheet was found. No crown was trimmed, torn or re-cut once it had been measured.
d.q: Why will six crowns not close? Argue for one cause.

sus.why: a sheet listing width across, where a head is measured around
no crown trimmed, torn or re-cut once measured
a last roll two inches narrower than the first
two sheets in the folder, the older one for a smaller size

evidence: “The pattern sheet lists the head width across instead of the distance around.”
“A circle's distance around is a little more than three times its width.”
args.against: “Two pattern sheets sit in the folder and the older one is for a smaller size.”

evidence: “The card ran out and the last roll is two inches narrower than the first.”
“The six that failed were all cut by the same two students.”
args.against: “The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need.”

evidence: “Two pattern sheets sit in the folder and the older one is for a smaller size.”
“The six failed crowns were cut on the afternoon the second sheet was found.”
args.against: “A circle's distance around is a little more than three times its width.”

clears: Trimming them too short: “No crown was trimmed, torn or re-cut once it had been measured.”
d.note: A third is the number that decides this and the class should go to it straight away. Two inches off a roll is not a third of a crown. A smaller pattern might be, and the case never says how much smaller. Only the width-for-circumference mistake lands near a third on the arithmetic alone.

title: The Case of the Piano That Went Sour
story: The music room piano was tuned in October and sounded wrong by February. No other instrument in the building had shifted at all. Nobody had moved the piano and no string had broken. A piano string is stretched across a wooden frame that holds its tension. Wood takes in water from damp air and gives it up in dry air, swelling and shrinking as it does. A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once. The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February. The other instruments live in cases that hold their own air. The tuner found every string flat by about the same amount.
q: Why did the piano go out of tune?

sus.who: 💨 Dry winter air shrinking the frame
sus.why: a frame that shrinks lets every string go slack at once
nobody had moved the piano

sus.who: 🎻 A problem in the whole building
sus.why: no other instrument had shifted at all
no string had broken

ans: Dry February air shrank the wooden frame and loosened every string.
proof: “A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once.”
“The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February.”
clears: The piano being moved: “Nobody had moved the piano and no string had broken.”
The whole building: “No other instrument in the building had shifted at all.”
A broken string: “no string had broken.”
explain: Every string went flat by the same amount, which no single broken string can do. Because the humidity fell from fifty-five percent to nineteen, the frame holding all of them shrank and let the whole set go slack together.

d.story: The music room piano was tuned in October and sounded wrong by February. A piano string is stretched across a wooden frame that holds its tension. Wood takes in water from damp air and gives it up in dry air, swelling and shrinking as it does. A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once. The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February. The tuner found every string flat by about the same amount. The piano was rolled to the hall for the winter concert and back again. One bass string was found with a loose coil at its tuning pin. A slack string pulls the frame out of balance and drags its neighbours flat. The other instruments all live in cases that hold their own air.
d.q: Why did the piano go flat? Choose one cause and quote the story.

sus.who: 💨 Dry winter air shrinking the frame
sus.why: fifty-five percent humidity in October against nineteen in February
rolled to the hall for the concert and back again

sus.who: 🎻 A problem in the whole building
sus.why: other instruments living in cases that hold their own air
a loose coil at a bass tuning pin

evidence: “The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February.”
“A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once.”
args.against: “The piano was rolled to the hall for the winter concert and back again.”

evidence: “The piano was rolled to the hall for the winter concert and back again.”
“The tuner found every string flat by about the same amount.”
args.against: “Wood takes in water from damp air and gives it up in dry air, swelling and shrinking as it does.”

evidence: “One bass string was found with a loose coil at its tuning pin.”
“A slack string pulls the frame out of balance and drags its neighbours flat.”
args.against: “The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February.”

clears: A problem in the whole building: “The other instruments all live in cases that hold their own air.”
d.note: Every string flat by about the same amount is the sentence that carries this case, and all three open answers now claim it. Dry air slackens the frame, a trip jolts the whole instrument, and one loose string can drag its neighbours. Ask which of the three would leave the bass worse than the treble, because the story says it did not.

title: The Case of the Kite That Would Not Climb
story: Two identical kites flew on the same afternoon and only one would climb. Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string. The flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon. A kite climbs on air that moves steadily in one direction. A building sends the wind over its roof and leaves a churning pocket behind it. That pocket pushes up, down and sideways by turns instead of steadily. The kite that failed was flown on the lawn right behind the gym. The one that climbed was flown in the open field beyond the gym. A ribbon held up on the lawn flapped in every direction at once.
q: Why would one kite not climb?

sus.why: a ribbon on the lawn flapped in every direction at once
the flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon
both were built from the same kit
the same tail and string on both

ans: The gym churned the wind on the lawn so the kite had no steady air.
proof: “A building sends the wind over its roof and leaves a churning pocket behind it.”
“That pocket pushes up, down and sideways by turns instead of steadily.”
clears: No wind: “The flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon.”
A badly built kite: “Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string.”
The tail: “Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string.”
explain: There was plenty of wind and two identical kites. Because the gym leaves a churning pocket behind it, the kite on the lawn was pushed four ways at once while the one in the open field had steady air to climb on.

d.story: Two kites flew on the same afternoon and only one would climb. A kite climbs on air that moves steadily in one direction. A building sends the wind over its roof and leaves a churning pocket behind it. That pocket pushes up, down and sideways by turns instead of steadily. The kite that failed was flown on the lawn right behind the gym. The one that climbed was flown in the open field beyond the gym. A ribbon held up on the lawn flapped in every direction at once. The failed kite's spine is bowed and its two halves no longer match. A kite with one half larger than the other turns instead of climbing. The failed kite's tail had been tied to the wrong corner that morning. The flag on the gym roof stood straight out the whole afternoon.
d.q: Why would one kite not climb? Make the case for one cause.

sus.why: a churning pocket behind the gym, and a ribbon flapping every way
a roof flag standing straight out the whole afternoon
a bowed spine, with the two halves no longer matching
a tail tied to the wrong corner that morning

evidence: “The kite that failed was flown on the lawn right behind the gym.”
“A ribbon held up on the lawn flapped in every direction at once.”
args.against: “The failed kite's spine is bowed and its two halves no longer match.”

evidence: “The failed kite's spine is bowed and its two halves no longer match.”
“A kite with one half larger than the other turns instead of climbing.”
args.against: “A ribbon held up on the lawn flapped in every direction at once.”

evidence: “The failed kite's tail had been tied to the wrong corner that morning.”
“The one that climbed was flown in the open field beyond the gym.”
args.against: “That pocket pushes up, down and sideways by turns instead of steadily.”

clears: No wind that day: “The flag on the gym roof stood straight out the whole afternoon.”
d.note: The ribbon is a measurement somebody actually took and it is the best thing in the story. It describes the lawn, though, not the kite, so it argues for the place rather than against the build. The cheapest test is already in the case: swap the two kites between the two spots and fly them again.

title: The Case of the Shamrock That Closed at Four
story: The shamrock plant on the sill folded its leaves shut every afternoon at four. It opened again each morning without anyone touching it. The soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted. No insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf. Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light. The folding happens on schedule whether or not the plant is short of water. A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on. Before January the sill held direct light until nearly seven. A second shamrock in the sunnier window folds at close to seven instead.
q: Why does the shamrock close at four?

sus.why: some plants fold their leaves on a rhythm set by light
the soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted
no insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf
it opened again each morning without anyone touching it

ans: The new shed cuts the light that sets the plant's folding rhythm.
proof: “Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light.”
“A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on.”
clears: Dry soil: “The soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted.”
Pests or disease: “No insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf.”
Somebody touching it: “It opened again each morning without anyone touching it.”
explain: The second shamrock is the control. Because the sunnier window still holds light until seven and folds at seven, the plant on the shaded sill is reading the shed, not thirst or damage.

d.story: The shamrock plant on the sill folded its leaves shut every afternoon at four. It opened again each morning on its own. Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light. A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on. A second shamrock in the sunnier window folds at close to seven instead. The radiator under the sill cycles on at four and dries that soil fastest then. A shamrock folds its leaves to hold water in when the soil goes dry. The cleaner wipes that sill at four each afternoon before she leaves. A shamrock will also fold when a leaf is brushed or knocked. Not a leaf showed insect damage, mold or a mark of any kind.
d.q: Why does the shamrock fold at four? Pick one cause and prove it.

sus.why: a shed blocking the sill from three, where light once lasted later
a radiator cycling on at four and drying that soil
no insect damage, mold or mark on any leaf
a cleaner wiping that sill at four each afternoon

evidence: “A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on.”
“A second shamrock in the sunnier window folds at close to seven instead.”
args.against: “The cleaner wipes that sill at four each afternoon before she leaves.”

evidence: “The radiator under the sill cycles on at four and dries that soil fastest then.”
“A shamrock folds its leaves to hold water in when the soil goes dry.”
args.against: “It opened again each morning on its own.”

evidence: “The cleaner wipes that sill at four each afternoon before she leaves.”
“A shamrock will also fold when a leaf is brushed or knocked.”
args.against: “Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light.”

clears: Pests or disease: “Not a leaf showed insect damage, mold or a mark of any kind.”
d.note: The second shamrock is the strongest evidence and it is worth slowing down on. It folds at seven in a sunnier window, which ties the folding to light rather than to the hour of four. Both other answers land exactly on four, and a student who notices that a clock-time match is weaker than a light match has read well.

title: The Case of the Puddle That Stayed
story: One puddle on the field lasted nine days and every other puddle dried in two. All of them filled during the same Saturday rain. The long puddle sits in a shallow dip only two inches deep. Water leaves the ground by soaking down or drying off the top. Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil. A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay. Samples from the other spots came up brown and sandy. Sun and wind reached every part of the field equally all nine days. The dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream.
q: Why did one puddle last nine days?

sus.why: a core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay
the dip is only two inches deep
the dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream
sun and wind reached every part of the field equally

ans: Clay soil under the dip let the water soak down very slowly.
proof: “Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil.”
“A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay.”
clears: A deeper hole: “The long puddle sits in a shallow dip only two inches deep.”
Water feeding in: “The dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream.”
Less sun: “Sun and wind reached every part of the field equally all nine days.”
explain: It is the shallowest puddle and it lasted longest, so depth is not the answer. Because the soil under it is packed clay while the rest of the field is sandy, the water had almost no way down.

d.story: One puddle on the field lasted nine days and every other puddle dried in two. All of them filled during the same Saturday rain. Water leaves the ground by soaking down or drying off the top. Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil. A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay. Samples from the other spots came up brown and sandy. The dip is the lowest point on the field and the ground slopes to it from three sides. Rain that falls anywhere on that slope ends up in the dip. The dip sits in the shadow of the equipment shed from noon onward. A shaded puddle loses far less water off its top than a sunlit one. The dip is a shallow one, two inches at its deepest point.
d.q: Why did one puddle last nine days? Choose one cause and back it up.

sus.why: grey packed clay in the dip where the others came up sandy
two inches at its deepest point
the lowest point, with ground sloping to it from three sides
shade from the equipment shed from noon onward

evidence: “A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay.”
“Samples from the other spots came up brown and sandy.”
args.against: “The dip sits in the shadow of the equipment shed from noon onward.”

evidence: “The dip is the lowest point on the field and the ground slopes to it from three sides.”
“Rain that falls anywhere on that slope ends up in the dip.”
args.against: “All of them filled during the same Saturday rain.”

evidence: “The dip sits in the shadow of the equipment shed from noon onward.”
“A shaded puddle loses far less water off its top than a sunlit one.”
args.against: “Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil.”

clears: A deeper hole: “The dip is a shallow one, two inches at its deepest point.”
d.note: The story names the two ways water leaves the ground, and the open answers split neatly across them: clay blocks the way down, shade blocks the way off the top, and the slope keeps topping it up. Sorting the suspects into those three jobs before choosing is the method this case teaches.

title: The Case of the Seeds That Never Came Up
story: Two rows of sunflower seeds went in on the same morning and one row sprouted. Both rows came from the same packet, dated this year. Both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule. A seed carries only enough stored food to push a shoot a short way up. A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light. The sprouting row was planted half an inch down as the packet says. The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel. Dug up three weeks later, the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground. The soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth.
q: Why did one row never come up?

sus.why: a seed buried too deep runs out of food before reaching light
the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground
both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule
the soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth

ans: The deep row sprouted underground and ran out of food before surfacing.
proof: “A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light.”
“The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel.”
clears: Dead seed: “Dug up three weeks later, the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground.”
Too little water: “Both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule.”
Cold soil: “The soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth.”
explain: The seeds were alive — they germinated. Because four inches is further than a sunflower's stored food can push a shoot, the row sprouted and then starved before it ever reached the surface.

d.story: Two rows of sunflower seeds went in on the same morning and one row sprouted. A seed carries only enough stored food to push a shoot a short way up. A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light. The sprouting row was planted half an inch down as the packet says. The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel. Three weeks on, the dug-up deep seeds had sprouted and then died below ground. The second row runs along the fence where the ground stays cold until May. The deep row was watered by hose and the shallow row by watering can. A hose on packed ground runs off rather than soaking in. Both rows came from one packet, dated this year.
d.q: Why did one row never come up? Argue for one cause.

sus.why: four inches down, where a seed runs out of food before the light
one packet, dated this year, for both rows
a hose on packed ground that runs off rather than soaking in
along the fence, where the ground stays cold until May

evidence: “The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel.”
“Three weeks on, the dug-up deep seeds had sprouted and then died below ground.”
args.against: “The second row runs along the fence where the ground stays cold until May.”

evidence: “The deep row was watered by hose and the shallow row by watering can.”
“A hose on packed ground runs off rather than soaking in.”
args.against: “A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light.”

evidence: “The second row runs along the fence where the ground stays cold until May.”
“A seed carries only enough stored food to push a shoot a short way up.”
args.against: “The sprouting row was planted half an inch down as the packet says.”

clears: Dead seed: “Both rows came from one packet, dated this year.”
d.note: Sprouted and then died below ground is the fact that beats most of this. Seeds that sprouted were not too cold and were not too dry, because both of those stop a seed before it starts. Depth is the only suspect that lets a seed begin and then run out, and reasoning from when the seed failed is the whole trick.

title: The Case of the Egg That Floated
story: Six eggs went into a bowl of water and one floated while five sank. All six came from the same farm and the same carton. None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything. An egg has a small air pocket at its blunt end just inside the shell. The shell is slightly porous, so water leaves the egg slowly and air takes its place. The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows. An egg floats once its air pocket is large enough to lift it. Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier. The five sinking eggs all carried this week's stamp.
q: Why did one egg float?

sus.who: 🫧 A grown air pocket in an older egg
sus.why: an egg floats once its air pocket is large enough
none of them was cracked
all six came from the same farm and the same carton
none of them was warm

ans: The floating egg was five weeks older and its air pocket had grown.
proof: “The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows.”
“Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier.”
clears: A cracked shell: “None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything.”
A different farm: “All six came from the same farm and the same carton.”
Being warm: “None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything.”
explain: One carton, one farm, five weeks of difference. Because water leaves an egg slowly and air replaces it, the oldest egg carries the biggest air pocket, and that is what lifted it off the bottom.

d.story: Six eggs went into a bowl of water and one floated while five sank. An egg has a small air pocket at its blunt end just inside the shell. The shell is slightly porous, so water leaves the egg slowly and air takes its place. The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows. An egg floats once its air pocket is large enough to lift it. Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier. The five sinking eggs all carried this week's stamp. The floating egg has a hairline crack across its blunt end. A cracked shell lets air in far faster than a sound one does. The floating egg had sat on the warm windowsill since Tuesday. All six came out of one carton from one farm.
d.q: Why did one egg float? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.who: 🫧 A grown air pocket in an older egg
sus.why: a date stamp five weeks older than the other five
a hairline crack across its blunt end
one carton from one farm for all six
sitting on the warm windowsill since Tuesday

evidence: “Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier.”
“The five sinking eggs all carried this week's stamp.”
args.against: “The floating egg has a hairline crack across its blunt end.”

evidence: “The floating egg has a hairline crack across its blunt end.”
“A cracked shell lets air in far faster than a sound one does.”
args.against: “An egg has a small air pocket at its blunt end just inside the shell.”

evidence: “The floating egg had sat on the warm windowsill since Tuesday.”
“The shell is slightly porous, so water leaves the egg slowly and air takes its place.”
args.against: “The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows.”

clears: A different farm: “All six came out of one carton from one farm.”
d.note: Age, a crack and warmth all enlarge the same air pocket, so this is not three answers but three routes to one. Say that, then argue about speed: five weeks is slow and sure, a crack is fast, and four warm days sits between. The crack is also the one fact that might have been caused by the others rather than causing them.

title: The Case of the Shadow That Moved House
story: A class marked the flagpole's noon shadow in September and remeasured in December. The September mark sat eleven feet from the base and the December mark nineteen. Nobody moved the flagpole and the ground was checked for settling. Both measurements were taken at local noon from the same chalk cross. The sun rides lower in the sky in winter than it does in autumn. A lower sun throws a longer shadow from the same object. A sun-angle table gave fifty-two degrees in September and thirty-one in December. The pole's height was measured both times at twenty-nine feet. The weather was clear and still on both measuring days.
q: Why was the December shadow so much longer?

sus.why: a lower sun throws a longer shadow from the same object
nobody moved the flagpole and the ground was checked
both were taken at local noon from the same chalk cross
the pole's height was measured both times at twenty-nine feet

ans: The December sun sat twenty-one degrees lower and stretched the shadow.
proof: “The sun rides lower in the sky in winter than it does in autumn.”
“A sun-angle table gave fifty-two degrees in September and thirty-one in December.”
clears: The flagpole moving: “Nobody moved the flagpole and the ground was checked for settling.”
A measuring mistake: “Both measurements were taken at local noon from the same chalk cross.”
The pole getting taller: “The pole's height was measured both times at twenty-nine feet.”
explain: Same pole, same spot, same hour. Because the sun sat fifty-two degrees up in September and only thirty-one in December, the identical twenty-nine-foot pole threw a shadow eight feet longer.

d.story: A class marked the flagpole's noon shadow in September and remeasured in December. The September mark sat eleven feet from the base and the December mark nineteen. The sun rides lower in the sky in winter than it does in autumn. A lower sun throws a longer shadow from the same object. A sun-angle table gave fifty-two degrees in September and thirty-one in December. The September reading was taken at clock noon and the December one at local noon. Clock noon and local noon can be most of an hour apart in December. The base was re-concreted in November and the pole now stands a foot nearer the wall. Both marks were measured out from the same chalk cross on the path. The pole's height was measured at twenty-nine feet on both days.
d.q: Why did the shadow grow eight feet? Choose one cause and back it up.

sus.why: fifty-two degrees in September against thirty-one in December
re-concreted in November, standing a foot nearer the wall
clock noon in September and local noon in December
twenty-nine feet on both measuring days

evidence: “The sun rides lower in the sky in winter than it does in autumn.”
“A sun-angle table gave fifty-two degrees in September and thirty-one in December.”
args.against: “The September reading was taken at clock noon and the December one at local noon.”

evidence: “The base was re-concreted in November and the pole now stands a foot nearer the wall.”
“Both marks were measured out from the same chalk cross on the path.”
args.against: “A lower sun throws a longer shadow from the same object.”

evidence: “The September reading was taken at clock noon and the December one at local noon.”
“Clock noon and local noon can be most of an hour apart in December.”
args.against: “A sun-angle table gave fifty-two degrees in September and thirty-one in December.”

clears: The pole getting taller: “The pole's height was measured at twenty-nine feet on both days.”
d.note: The sun really is lower and the table proves it, so the honest question is not whether the shadow grew but whether it grew by eight feet. A moved base and a mistimed noon both push the same way and neither was corrected for. A strong answer works out roughly how much of the eight feet the angle alone accounts for.

title: The Case of the Blurred Runner
story: Every photo from the track meet came out sharp except the ones of the runners. The fences, the clouds and the seated crowd were all crisp in the same frames. The lens was clean and the camera sat locked on a tripod. A camera makes a picture by holding its shutter open for a slice of time. Anything that moves while the shutter is open smears across the picture. The settings log shows a shutter held open for a full quarter second. A sprinter covers about seven feet in a quarter of a second. The photographer used the same settings for every shot that day. The focus ring was taped in place before the meet began.
q: Why were only the runners blurred?

sus.who: ⏱️ A shutter held open a quarter second
sus.why: a sprinter covers about seven feet in that time
the camera sat locked on a tripod
the focus ring was taped in place before the meet
the lens was clean

ans: The shutter stayed open long enough for the runners to move across it.
proof: “Anything that moves while the shutter is open smears across the picture.”
“The settings log shows a shutter held open for a full quarter second.”
clears: A shaky camera: “The lens was clean and the camera sat locked on a tripod.”
Bad focus: “The focus ring was taped in place before the meet began.”
A dirty lens: “The lens was clean and the camera sat locked on a tripod.”
explain: Everything still is sharp and everything moving is not, in the very same frames. Because the shutter stayed open a quarter second and a sprinter crosses seven feet in that time, only the runners smeared.

d.story: Every photo from the track meet came out sharp except the ones of the runners. The fences, the clouds and the seated crowd were all crisp in the same frames. A camera makes a picture by holding its shutter open for a slice of time. Anything that moves while the shutter is open smears across the picture. The settings log shows a shutter held open for a full quarter second. A sprinter covers about seven feet in a quarter of a second. The photographer took the camera off the tripod and panned it by hand after the first race. A hand-panned camera never matches a runner's speed exactly. The autofocus was set to lock on the nearest object, which was the rail. The front of the lens was wiped and checked before the first race.
d.q: Why are only the runners blurred? Make the case for one cause.

sus.who: ⏱️ A shutter held open a quarter second
sus.why: a quarter-second shutter, with a sprinter covering seven feet
taken off the tripod and panned by hand after the first race
autofocus locked on the nearest object, which was the rail
a lens wiped and checked before the first race

evidence: “The settings log shows a shutter held open for a full quarter second.”
“A sprinter covers about seven feet in a quarter of a second.”
args.against: “The photographer took the camera off the tripod and panned it by hand after the first race.”

evidence: “The photographer took the camera off the tripod and panned it by hand after the first race.”
“A hand-panned camera never matches a runner's speed exactly.”
args.against: “The fences, the clouds and the seated crowd were all crisp in the same frames.”

evidence: “The autofocus was set to lock on the nearest object, which was the rail.”
“Anything that moves while the shutter is open smears across the picture.”
args.against: “A sprinter covers about seven feet in a quarter of a second.”

clears: A dirty lens: “The front of the lens was wiped and checked before the first race.”
d.note: Crisp fences in the same frame is the fact that does the most work, and it cuts hard against panning: a panned camera smears the background, not the subject. Point that out only after the class has argued it. The focus answer has to explain why the crowd, further away than the rail, came out sharp.

title: The Case of the Leaning Bean Plant
story: A bean plant on the counter leaned hard toward the window by Friday. It had stood straight on Monday and nobody had tipped the pot. The stem was firm and green with no sign of rot or breakage. The soil was level and the pot sat flat on the counter. A plant grows the cells on its shaded side longer than those on its lit side. Growing longer on one side only is what bends a stem toward light. The window is the room's only light source and sits to the plant's left. A second bean under a lamp directly overhead stood perfectly straight all week. Both plants had the same soil, water and pot.
q: Why did the bean plant lean?

sus.why: growing longer on one side only bends a stem toward light
the soil was level and the pot sat flat on the counter
the stem was firm and green with no sign of rot
both plants had the same soil, water and pot

ans: One-sided light made the shaded side of the stem grow longer.
proof: “A plant grows the cells on its shaded side longer than those on its lit side.”
“The window is the room's only light source and sits to the plant's left.”
clears: A tipped pot: “The soil was level and the pot sat flat on the counter.”
Rot in the stem: “The stem was firm and green with no sign of rot or breakage.”
Uneven watering: “Both plants had the same soil, water and pot.”
explain: The bean under the overhead lamp is the control and it stood straight. Because light reaching a stem from one side makes the shaded cells grow longer than the lit ones, the stem bends — it is growth, not damage or a tilt.

d.story: A bean plant on the counter leaned hard toward the window by Friday. A plant grows the cells on its shaded side longer than those on its lit side. Growing longer on one side only is what bends a stem toward light. The window is the room's only light source and sits to the plant's left. A second bean under a lamp directly overhead stood perfectly straight all week. The counter itself slopes a finger's width down toward the window. A pot that sits on a slope leans, and the stem leans with it. The watering can is always tipped in from the window side of the pot. Roots grow toward the wetter side and pull the stem over with them. The stem is firm and green with no soft spot or break anywhere.
d.q: Why does the bean plant lean? Pick one cause and quote the story.

sus.why: a window on its left as the room's only light
a counter sloping a finger's width toward the window
a stem firm and green, with no soft spot or break
a can always tipped in from the window side

evidence: “The window is the room's only light source and sits to the plant's left.”
“A second bean under a lamp directly overhead stood perfectly straight all week.”
args.against: “The counter itself slopes a finger's width down toward the window.”

evidence: “The counter itself slopes a finger's width down toward the window.”
“A pot that sits on a slope leans, and the stem leans with it.”
args.against: “Growing longer on one side only is what bends a stem toward light.”

evidence: “The watering can is always tipped in from the window side of the pot.”
“Roots grow toward the wetter side and pull the stem over with them.”
args.against: “A plant grows the cells on its shaded side longer than those on its lit side.”

clears: Rot in the stem: “The stem is firm and green with no soft spot or break anywhere.”
d.note: Light, slope and watering all pull the same way, which the story arranges deliberately. The lamp-lit twin is a control and a partial one: it sits on the same sloping counter, so it argues against the light being necessary without clearing the slope. Ask what a spirit level and a turned pot would each settle.

title: The Case of the Ice Cream in the Metal Bowl
story: Two scoops came out of the freezer together and the metal bowl's scoop melted first. The plastic bowl's scoop still held its shape twenty minutes later. Both scoops were the same size from the same tub. Both bowls sat side by side on the same table in the same room. Heat moves into ice cream from whatever is touching it. Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does. The room and both bowls had been sitting at seventy-one degrees all morning. Neither bowl was in sunlight and neither had been warmed or rinsed. A thermometer read seventy-one inside both bowls before the scoops went in.
q: Why did the metal bowl's ice cream melt first?

sus.why: metal carries heat many times faster than plastic
neither bowl was in sunlight
both bowls had been sitting at seventy-one degrees all morning
both scoops were the same size from the same tub

ans: The metal bowl moved room heat into the ice cream far faster.
proof: “Heat moves into ice cream from whatever is touching it.”
“Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does.”
clears: Sunlight: “Neither bowl was in sunlight and neither had been warmed or rinsed.”
A warm bowl: “A thermometer read seventy-one inside both bowls before the scoops went in.”
A bigger scoop: “Both scoops were the same size from the same tub.”
explain: Both bowls started at the same seventy-one degrees, so it is not that one was warmer. Because metal passes that heat along many times faster than plastic, the same room melts one scoop long before the other.

d.story: Two scoops came out of the freezer together and the metal bowl's scoop melted first. The plastic bowl's scoop still held its shape twenty minutes later. Heat moves into ice cream from whatever is touching it. Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does. A patch of sun crosses the table from ten until noon and reaches only the metal bowl. Sunlight falling on a bowl warms it whatever the bowl is made of. The metal bowl had been stacked above the dishwasher vent all morning. A bowl that starts warm hands its heat straight to what goes into it. Both scoops were weighed at ninety grams from the same tub.
d.q: Why did the metal bowl's scoop melt first? Choose one cause and prove it.

sus.why: metal carrying heat many times faster than plastic
a patch of sun reaching only the metal bowl
stacked above the dishwasher vent all morning
both weighed at ninety grams from one tub

evidence: “Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does.”
“Heat moves into ice cream from whatever is touching it.”
args.against: “The metal bowl had been stacked above the dishwasher vent all morning.”

evidence: “A patch of sun crosses the table from ten until noon and reaches only the metal bowl.”
“Sunlight falling on a bowl warms it whatever the bowl is made of.”
args.against: “Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does.”

evidence: “The metal bowl had been stacked above the dishwasher vent all morning.”
“A bowl that starts warm hands its heat straight to what goes into it.”
args.against: “The plastic bowl's scoop still held its shape twenty minutes later.”

clears: A bigger scoop: “Both scoops were weighed at ninety grams from the same tub.”
d.note: Two of the three answers say the metal bowl was already warm and one says it merely carries heat well. That is a real distinction and the class should make it, because it points at different tests. Measuring both bowls with a thermometer before the scoops go in settles two suspects at once.

title: The Case of the Ribbon That Lost Its Red
story: A long red ribbon on the fence faded to pale pink along one stretch only. The faded stretch runs the length of the south-facing side. The rest of the ribbon, on the north side, is still deep red. It is one continuous ribbon tied at both ends and never cut. Sunlight breaks down the dyes in fabric and lightens the color over time. The south side of this fence takes direct sun from morning until evening. The north side sits in the building's shadow for most of the day. No rain, cleaner or bleach reached one side more than the other. The ribbon was one color when it was tied up in April.
q: Why did only part of the ribbon fade?

sus.why: the south side takes direct sun from morning until evening
no cleaner or bleach reached one side more than the other
it is one continuous ribbon tied at both ends and never cut
no rain reached one side more than the other

ans: Sunlight broke down the red dye on the south-facing stretch.
proof: “Sunlight breaks down the dyes in fabric and lightens the color over time.”
“The south side of this fence takes direct sun from morning until evening.”
clears: Bleach or cleaner: “No rain, cleaner or bleach reached one side more than the other.”
Two ribbons: “It is one continuous ribbon tied at both ends and never cut.”
Rain: “No rain, cleaner or bleach reached one side more than the other.”
explain: One ribbon, never cut, two colors. Because the faded stretch is exactly the stretch that takes sun all day and the deep red stretch sits in shadow, the sun is the only thing that differs along its length.

d.story: A long red ribbon on the fence faded to pale pink along one stretch only. The faded stretch runs the length of the south-facing side. title: The Case of the Balloons That Sank Overnight
story: Thirty foil balloons touched the gym ceiling on Friday and rested on the floor on Monday. None of them had popped and every knot still held. Foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil. A gas shrinks when it cools and takes up less room than it did warm. A balloon floats only while it pushes aside more air than it weighs. A balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating. The gym heat is switched off from Friday evening until Monday morning. A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday. Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.
q: Why did the balloons sink?
